summary: The new module captures delegation facts in the ledger, but the key limits are not actually enforced on child execution, and there are two concurrency bugs around reservation/grant timing. `sweep_stale()` also has broader side effects than its API suggests.

findings.message: `spawn()` computes `iterations` and filtered `caps`, but the child is submitted as a plain scheduler job with only `command`/`priority`/`timeout_s`/`lane`. The runner later executes only the claimed manifest, and nothing in the existing scheduler/runner path reads `DELEGATION_GRANTED`. As written, the delegation limits are only ledgered, not enforced: a child still runs with the default environment and no actual iteration cap.

There is a race between `Scheduler.submit()` and the later `DELEGATION_GRANTED` append. `submit()` makes the child immediately claimable, so another worker can start running it before the delegation metadata exists. If that child delegates during this window, `depth_of(child)` returns 0 and the max-depth / `delegate` stripping logic is bypassed.

A crash or kill after `append_guarded()` records `DELEGATION_RESERVED` but before `DELEGATION_RELEASED`/`DELEGATION_GRANTED` leaves the reservation permanently open. Concurrency accounting treats open reservations as live children, so one interrupted spawn can consume a slot forever and eventually block all future delegation for that parent.

`sweep_stale()` claims to report stale delegated children only, but it calls `self.sched.report_stale(older_than_s)`, which marks every stale running job in the scheduler as `JOB_STALE` before filtering the return value. Calling this helper from delegation code will mutate unrelated jobs' state as a side effect.
